questions.stem: A 68-year-old female presents with a severe headache, jaw claudication, and vision changes, including transient episodes of visual loss in the left eye. On physical examination, the left temporal artery is tender to palpation and appears swollen. Laboratory tests reveal elevated ESR and C-reactive protein (CRP). A biopsy of the temporal artery is performed, which shows transmural inflammation with multinucleated giant cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. A. Temporal arteritis

questions.stem: A 52-year-old male presents with severe abdominal pain, weight loss, and hypertension. He reports a history of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. Physical examination reveals livedo reticularis, digital gangrene, and multiple abdominal bruits. Laboratory tests show an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), elevated serum creatinine, and a positive HBV surface antigen (HBsAg). A renal biopsy demonstrates necrotizing arteritis with fibrinoid necrosis. Which of the following vasculitides is most likely responsible for these findings?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. A. Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man presents to the emergency room with acute chest pain. The ECG is normal. Analysis of which pair of serum markers given below would be most helpful in excluding a diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. C. CK-MB and cardiac troponin-I

questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension undergoes renal biopsy for evaluation of chronic renal disease. The biopsy is shown in the image. What is the appropriate diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. A. Hyaline arteriolosclerosis

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with diabetes presents with a history of progressive pain in both legs for several years. The pain is severe after walking two blocks or climbing one flight of stairs. Blood pressure is 146/90 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show a serum cholesterol of 300 mg/dL. He neither smokes nor drinks. Bruits are evident upon auscultation of both femoral arteries. The pathogenesis of intermittent claudication in this patient is most closely associated with which of the following risk factors?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Hyperlipidemia

 

Intermittent claudication is a classic symptom of peripheral artery disease (PAD), which is most commonly caused by atherosclerosis of the large and medium-sized arteries of the lower limbs. The symptoms (leg pain on exertion relieved by rest) are due to inadequate blood flow to the muscles during exercise.

 

Pathogenesis:

 

  • Atherosclerosis results from lipid accumulation in the arterial walls, triggering chronic inflammation and plaque formation.
  • This leads to luminal narrowing, reducing blood supply especially during increased demand (e.g., walking).
  • In this patient, bruits in femoral arteries and exercise-induced pain are classic for PAD.

 

Risk Factors for Atherosclerosis (and thus PAD):

 

Major:

 

  • Hyperlipidemia (especially high LDL cholesterol – patient’s cholesterol is 300 mg/dL!)
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Smoking (absent here)
  • Hypertension
  • Contributory:
  • Sedentary lifestyle
  • Obesity
  • Age
  • Male sex

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hyperglycemia: A major contributor to microvascular disease and a secondary risk factor for atherosclerosis, but hyperlipidemia is more directly linked to the initiation and progression of atherosclerosis.

 

Option C. Obesity and sedentary lifestyle: Risk factors, but less directly implicated in the pathogenesis of the arterial plaque itself.

 

Option D. Systemic hypertension: Contributes to endothelial dysfunction and promotes atherosclerosis, but again hyperlipidemia is the most critical driver in PAD.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man has come to a hospital for routine screening. His physician notes calcification in the wall of the radial artery, which otherwise appears unremarkable. Which of the following is the appropriate diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Mönckeberg medial sclerosis

 

Mönckeberg medial sclerosis (also called medial calcific sclerosis) is characterized by:

 

  • Calcification of the tunica media of medium-sized muscular arteries (e.g., radial, ulnar arteries).
  • It does not significantly narrow the lumen → no clinical ischemia.
  • Often discovered incidentally on X-rays or physical examination as a palpable "pipestem" artery.
  • Most common in older adults.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)

 

  • A necrotizing vasculitis involving small- and medium-sized arteries.
  • Presents with systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss), renal involvement, abdominal pain, etc.
  • Arteries show transmural inflammation with fibrinoid necrosis, not just medial calcification.

 

Option B. Complicated atherosclerotic plaque

 

  • Involves intimal thickening, lipid core, and possibly calcification.
  • Causes luminal narrowing, ischemia, and clinical symptoms (e.g., angina, claudication).
  • Not limited to medial calcification and not asymptomatic.

 

Option C. Fibromuscular dysplasia

 

  • A non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory vascular disease.
  • Leads to stenosis and aneurysm, especially in renal and carotid arteries.
  • Seen mostly in younger women, not as incidental calcification in older men.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, intermittent arthritic pain of the knees, and abdominal pain. Physical examination reveals shallow ulcerations of the mucosa of the glans penis, as well as oral aphthous ulcers and conjunctivitis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. C. Behçet disease

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with increasing girth and fatigue. Physical examination reveals peripheral edema, ascites, and hepatomegaly. Liver function tests are normal. An echocardiogram shows a remarkably enlarged right heart and no signs of valvular heart disease. Endomyocardial biopsy discloses interstitial, pink amorphous deposits between cardiac myocytes. Which of the following is the appropriate diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. B. Cardiac amyloidosis.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman presents with a 1-hour history of substernal chest pain. Shortly after admission the patient expires. At autopsy, extensive calcium deposits are noted in the coronary and other arteries affected by severe atherosclerosis. Which of the following terms best describes these autopsy findings?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. A. Dystrophic calcification

questions.stem: A 45-year-old female presents with a history of recurrent embolic events to various organs, including the brain and extremities. On physical examination, there is a diastolic rumbling murmur heard best at the apex. An echocardiogram reveals a pedunculated mass attached to the left atrial septum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. C. Left atrial myxoma.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old male with a history of rheumatic heart disease presents with onset of high fever, chills, and confusion. On examination, there are multiple small, tender, erythematous nodules on his fingers and toes. Additionally, there are retinal hemorrhages noted on fundoscopic examination. Blood cultures are positive for a Gram-positive cocci in chains. Which of the following bacteria is the most likely causative organism for this patient's acute infective endocarditis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Streptococcus viridans

 

This patient presents with acute infective endocarditis in the context of rheumatic heart disease (which predisposes to valvular damage and vegetations). His symptoms and signs include:

 

  • High fever and confusion (systemic inflammatory response)
  • Osler nodes: tender, erythematous nodules on fingers/toes
  • Roth spots: retinal hemorrhages seen on fundoscopy
  • Positive blood cultures showing Gram-positive cocci in chains

 

These findings are classic for subacute bacterial endocarditis often caused by Streptococcus viridans, a group of alpha-hemolytic streptococci that are part of the normal oral flora. They can enter the bloodstream during dental procedures or through mucosal injury and colonize previously damaged heart valves, such as those affected by rheumatic heart disease.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Staphylococcus aureus: Causes acute endocarditis, especially on normal valves or in IV drug users. More aggressive with rapid valve destruction and septic emboli. It's Gram-positive cocci in clusters.

 

Option C. Streptococcus bovis (gallolyticus): Associated with colonic malignancies, commonly affects older adults. Blood cultures and colonic screening would be key here, but not the best fit in this scenario.

 

Option D. Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A strep): Not a common cause of endocarditis; more associated with pharyngitis, cellulitis, or necrotizing fasciitis.

questions.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer develops multiple organ dysfunction and expires. The heart at autopsy weighs 380 g (reference normal weight is 230-280g in women). The patient’s myocardium (right) is compared to normal myocardium (left). These pathologic findings are mostly likely due to which of the following conditions?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. D. Hypertension

questions.stemHtml: A 16-year-old college basketball player collapses on the court. A cardiac monitor shows ventricular tachycardia and then ventricular fibrillation. He is successfully resuscitated and hospitalized. The patient’s history indicates that his father died suddenly at 38 years of age. The boy’s echocardiogram reveals a thickened left ventricular wall, with a small slit-like chamber. The inter-ventricular septum is also markedly thickened. Five years later the patient expires suddenly. Histologic examination of the heart muscle at autopsy is shown in the image. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. D. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman underwent a mastectomy along with axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer 1 year back. Now she has developed swelling in left arm. Physical examination showed firm skin over left arm and doughy underlying soft tissue. Patient had complained of cellulitis in left arm 3 months back. Which of the following has likely diagnosis in this female?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Lymphedema

 

This patient has a history of mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection-a common cause of secondary lymphedema. Here's how her presentation aligns:

 

  • Key Clinical Clues:
    • Swelling of the left arm after breast cancer surgery
    • Firm skin with doughy soft tissue (classic for chronic lymphedema)
    • History of cellulitis-which both results from and exacerbates lymphedema

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Thrombophlebitis: Typically causes pain, redness, and cord-like veins, often in the legs. It’s not the classic post-mastectomy complication.

 

Option C. Vasculitis: Would present with systemic signs (fever, fatigue), palpable purpura, or skin ulcers—not just isolated arm swelling.

 

Option D. Tumor embolisation: Rare cause; would present with ischemia, sudden pain, or organ dysfunction, not gradual arm swelling.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Disruption or removal of axillary lymph nodes during mastectomy or lumpectomy, impairing lymphatic drainage from the arm.

 

Features:

 

  • Unilateral arm swelling (usually on the side of surgery)
  • Firm, doughy texture of subcutaneous tissue
  • Increased risk of cellulitis and recurrent infections
  • Can appear weeks to months—or even years—after surgery

 

Complications:

 

  • Chronic fibrosis
  • In rare cases, long-standing lymphedema can predispose to lymphangiosarcoma (known as Stewart-Treves syndrome)

questions.stem: The presence of stroke, peripheral vascular disease and atherosclerosis is associated with which hormone?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Insulin deficiency

 

Insulin deficiency is associated with diabetes mellitus which is responsible for stroke, peripheral vascular disease and atherosclerosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Hyperestrogenemia: Estrogen is generally cardioprotective (before menopause). Hyperestrogenemia isn't a classical cause of atherosclerosis.

 

Option C. Hypothyroidism: Less severe cause

 

Option D. Progesterone: Has minimal direct effect on vascular disease compared to estrogen or thyroid hormone.

questions.stem: Most common cause of abdominal aortic aneurysm is:
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. A. Atherosclerosis

questions.stem: Which is associated with vasculitis of medium size vessels?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Polyarteritis nodosa

 

Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is the classic vasculitis of medium-sized muscular arteries. It spares small vessels like arterioles, capillaries, and venules, and does not involve granulomas or ANCA (usually ANCA-negative).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Temporal arteritis (Giant Cell Arteritis): Affects large vessels, especially branches of the external carotid artery, such as the temporal artery.

 

Option B. Wegener’s granulomatosis (now called Granulomatosis with polyangiitis – GPA): Primarily affects small vessels (capillaries, venules, arterioles) and involves granulomatous inflammation. It is ANCA-positive (typically c-ANCA).

 

Option D. Henoch-Schönlein purpura (now called IgA vasculitis): Affects small vessels, especially in the skin, GI tract, and kidneys. It's an IgA-mediated small vessel vasculitis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Vasculitis Classification (Simplified):

 

  • Large vessel: Temporal arteritis, Takayasu arteritis
  • Medium vessel: Polyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki disease
  • Small vessel: GPA (Wegener's), MPA, EGPA, HSP (IgA vasculitis)

questions.stem: The mechanism of the development of Acute Rheumatic Fever is which of the following?

options.label: C
options.text: Due to toxin secretion by streptococci

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Cross reactivity with exogenous antigen

 

Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF) is a post-infectious autoimmune condition that follows infection with Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes). The key mechanism is:

 

  • Molecular mimicry / Cross-reactivity
  • Streptococcal M protein shares structural similarity with antigens in human tissues — especially heart, joints, skin, and brain.
  • The immune system produces antibodies against the streptococcal antigens, but those antibodies cross-react with host tissues.
  • This leads to inflammation and damage in the affected organs (e.g., pancarditis, arthritis, Sydenham chorea).

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Innocent bystander effect: Refers to tissue damage caused by immune responses that affect nearby normal tissues — not the primary mechanism in ARF.

 

Option C. Due to toxin secretion by streptococci: Toxins (like streptolysins or superantigens) are involved in conditions like scarlet fever or toxic shock, not ARF.

 

Option D. Release of pyrogenic cytokines: This contributes to fever in many infections but is not the underlying cause of rheumatic fever.

questions.stem: Most friable vegetation amongst the following options is seen in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Infective endocarditis

 

The hallmark of Infective endocarditis is the presence of friable, buly and potentially destructive vegetations containing fibrin, inflammatory cells and bacteria or other organisms on the heart valves.

 

The most friable vegetations, which are indicative of a high risk of embolization, are seen in infective endocarditis .

 

Friability refers to how easily a lesion breaks apart or embolizes. In cardiac vegetations, infective endocarditis (IE) is known to produce the most friable vegetations, due to their soft, necrotic, and loosely attached nature.

questions.stem: During autopsy of a patient died due to suspected myocardial infarction, the heart was stained with triphenyl tetrazolium tetra-chloride dye. What will be the color of the viable myocardium?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. D. Brick red
